title: Protocol to identify drug-binding sites in proteins using solution NMR spectroscopy
protocol: Clone the human p62 ZZ domain (aa 115–190) into a pGEX 6p-1 vector.
Transform the expression plasmid that encodes p62ZZ fused with GST tag into BL21 (DE3) RIL chemically competent cells according to the manufacturer’s protocol.
Plate the transformed cells onto LB agar plates supplemented with chloramphenicol and ampicillin.
Inoculate a single colony into 150 mL of LB media.
Culture the inoculated cells in an incubator shaker at 37°C and 200 rpm for 14–18 hours.
Dilute the overnight culture into 3 L of fresh LB media by adding 50 mL of cells to 1 liter of LB media.
Cultivate the diluted cells at 37°C with shaking at 200 rpm until an optical density of 0.3–0.4 is reached at 600 nm.
Reduce the temperature of the shaker to 16°C.

Centrifuge the cell culture using Beckman Coulter 500 mL polypropylene sterile bottles in a Thermo Scientific Sorvall RC 6 Plus Centrifuge with an F10-6×500 Fixed Angle Rotor at 3,500 rpm for 5 minutes.
Resuspend the cells with 50 mL M9 minimal media using a 50 mL pipette.
Transfer the resuspended cells back to 1 L M9 minimal media.
Weigh out 4 g of 13C-labeled glucose and dissolve in 30 mL M9 minimal media.
Weigh out 1 g of 15N-labeled NH4Cl and dissolve in 30 mL M9 minimal media.
Transfer the dissolved salts to the M9 minimal media.
Weigh out 0.1 g of vitamin power Centrum and dissolve in 40 mL Milli-Q water.
Remove undissolved solids by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm (4,424 × g) for 10 minutes at 4°C.
Filter the supernatant using a 0.22 μM Ezflow syringe filter.
Transfer the filtered vitamin solution to the M9 minimal media.
Add 0.2 mM IPTG into the M9 minimal media.
Induce protein expression at 16°C for 20 hours.
Harvest cells by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm (4,424 × g) for 10 minutes at 4°C using a F10-6×500 Fixed Angle Rotor in Thermo Scientific Sorvall RC 6 Plus Centrifuge.
Discard the supernatant and flash freeze the cell pellets in liquid nitrogen if storing at -80°C for up to 3 months.
Resuspend the cell pellets in 50 mL lysis buffer B by pipetting up and down using a transfer pipette.
Lysate the resuspended cells on ice by sonication for 10 minutes at 60% power with intervals of 5 seconds on and 10 seconds off using Q700CA SONICATOR attached to QSonica CL334 converter.
Spin down the cell lysate using Nalgene Oak Ridge centrifuge tubes at 14,000 g for 15 minutes at 4°C to remove cell debris and insoluble fractions.
Pass the supernatant to a 0.45 μm Syringe Filter (PALL) to remove residual cell debris completely.
Incubate the filtered solution with 2 mL Glutathione Agarose Resin in a 50 mL Falcon tube for 2 hours rocking on a Roto-Mini™ Rotator test tube rocker at 4°C.
Apply the suspension to an Econo-Pac® Chromatography Column (Bio-Rad) to collect the protein bound resin.
Wash the resin with 50 mL lysis buffer B supplemented with 100 mM arginine to remove impurities.
Resuspend the resin with 15 mL lysis buffer B, add home-made PreScission enzyme, and incubate the mixture rocking on a Labnet GyroMini™ Nutating Mixer for 4-24 hours at 4°C to cleave the GST tag.
Analyze a 10 μL sample of the PreScission cleavage reaction by polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE).
Once the desirable extent of the cleavage reaction is achieved (>80%), collect and concentrate the cleaved protein.
Apply the reaction mixture to an Econo-Pac gravity column (Bio-rad) to separate the beads.
Collect the flow-through, which contains the cleaved protein.
Centrifuge to remove potential precipitate and then concentrate the protein to 2 mL using a 3 kDa MWCO centrifugal filter at 4°C.
Inject the concentrated protein onto a PierceTM Protein Concentrator PES, 3 kDa pre-equilibrated in gel-filtration buffer supplemented with 100 mM arginine.
Run the sample at a flowrate of 0.4 mL/min.
Perform polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis using a 15-well homemade 15% gel.
Pool protein-containing fractions.
Concentrate pooled fractions to approximately 10 mg/mL using a 3 kDa MWCO centrifugal filter at 3,000 g.
Prepare the 13C/15N-labelled protein sample according to the protocol.
Add 8%–10% D2O to the protein sample (250 μL at 1.1 mM).
Supplement the buffer with 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.0), 100 mM NaCl, and 100 mM free arginine.
Load the prepared protein sample into a Shigemi NMR-tube using an NMR pipette.
Measure 1.5 μL of the protein sample at 280 nm to quantify concentration using a Nanodrop spectrometer.
Seal the Shigemi NMR microtube with parafilm to prevent evaporation during NMR experiments.
Execute the “topspin” command in the terminal or click on the topspin icon on the NMR instrument.
Open the topspin-gui.
Enter "ej" command in topspin-gui terminal.
Load the sample and enter "ij" to load the NMR sample onto the probe.
Create a new dataset using the command “iexpno”.
Use the command “rpar zg” to load the pulse sequence zg.
Set up the sample temperature to 298K using the edte panel (command: edte).
Equilibrate the temperature of the sample for 15 minutes.
Perform lock, tune and match using commands "lock" and "atma".
Auto-shim using command “topshim” as directed in the Bruker guide.
Calibrate the 90° pulse width for 1H (90° hard pulse) for the sample using standard calibration experiment.
Optional: Optimize the N15 and C13 pulse widths per instructions at local NMR facility.
Calibrate the water resonance frequency to set the o1p value.
Load the Bruker pulse sequences for 2D 1H-15N HSQC using command “rpar hsqcetf3gpsi” from Bruker library.
Load the Bruker pulse sequences for 1H-13C HSQC using command “rpar hsqcetgp” from Bruker library.
Adjust the carrier frequency using o2p (117 ppm) and spectral width SW (36 ppm) for 1H-15N HSQC.
Adjust the carrier frequency using o3p (43 ppm) and spectral width 84 ppm for 1H-13C HSQC.
Set number of scans (ns) and time domain points (TD) and other default parameters.
Acquire the 1H-15N HSQC data.
Process the acquired data using “xfb” command in the topspin terminal.
Adjust the phase in F1 dimension using the phase correction tab.
Adjust the phase in F2 dimension using the phase correction tab.
Acquire a set of 3D-NMR experiments [HNCACB, CBCA(CO)NH and HNCA].
Adjust parameters using the given table from Bruker library.
Use 1H-13C HSQC and 1H-15N HSQC experiments to adjust carrier frequency and spectral widths.
Perform 2D NMR before collecting 3D spectra to confirm protein folding, stability without aggregation or precipitation.
Ensure a well-dispersed 1H-15N HSQC spectrum with uniform intensity cross peaks.
Consult the local NMR facility for up-to-date pulse width and power level parameters.
Adjust receiver gain using “rga” command in topspin terminal.
Use “zg” command for individual experiment or “multizg” command to run all experiments.
Consult the local NMR facility to set up triple resonance experiments using non-uniform sampling (NUS) methods.
Monitor sample stability by running N15-HSQCs every day during data acquisition.
Process NMR data for backbone assignments using Topspin, NMRPipe, and CCPNMR/Assign on a Linux workstation or NMRbox account.
Open 3D NMR data in the topspin using menu tab or drag the NMR data into the topspin main GUI.
Use the "xfb" command to process data into 13 (CH) plane and 23 (NH) plane.
Correct phase correction in 1H, N15, and C13 planes.
Note down phase values in respective planes.
Use the “convert2pipe” command to open chemical shift reference window.
Select option depending on mode of data collection.
Generate a simple NMRPipe script for 3D NMR data using option 1.
Open fid.com file and click "ok" option.
Modify acquisition parameters including spectral, mode of acquisition, and phasing parameters in text file.
Enter noted phasing values in the text file.
Save the modified parameter file.
Change to c-shell using “csh” command.
Use “fid.com” command in 3D-NMR folder for each data type (HNCACB, CBCACONH, HNCA).
Process all 3D-NMR data using steps similar to previous ones.
Convert nmr data from pipe format into sparky format using pipe2ucsf xxxxxx.ft2 xxxx.ucsf command.
Open CCPNmr Analysis Assign module from terminal using “assign” command.
Select all .ucsf or .pipe files from the NMR data folder and drag them into the sidebar.
Load the spectrums using the “ls” command and open a tab to navigate the folder containing the NMR data files.
Drag and drop the 15N-HSQC, CBCAcoNH, HNCACB & HNCA spectra anywhere on the purple box in the drop box area.
Right-click on each spectrum and click on contours or use the command CO.
Uncheck the negative contours except for HNCACB spectra.
Adjust the contour levels to minimize the noise levels for all spectra.
Click on the 15N-HSQC spectrum and use Ctrl (or Cmd for Mac) + Shift + Left-drag on the contour to create the blue box in the region.
Release the button and keys to select the peaks or perform auto peak picking using shortcut PP.
Define spectral regions for N & H to select the positive peaks in 15N-HSQC spectra.
Inspect the peaks in 15N-HSQC spectrum and remove the noise peaks and sidechain peaks.
Use the shortcut SN command to create default peak labels for picked peaks in the previous step.
Toggle between different ways to display the peak labels using the shortcut PL.
Double click on the index number that makes changes in module tab which allows connecting CA (i-1), CB(i-1) and CA (i), CB(i) of i-1, i, i+1 residues.
Inspect sequential connection using Spin Graph assigner until all sequential assignments of residues are completed.
Open Assignment Inspector module to check connectivity of all residues in the given protein sequence.
Calculate CSPs in NMR titration experiments.
Plot CSPs as a histogram.
Mix ligands to induce specific binding effects on target protein crosspeaks.
Monitor changes in solvent environment due to ligand addition.
Observe saturation of CSPs with increasing ligand concentration.
Input processed NMR spectra of apo-formed p62ZZ and p62ZZ bound to various peptides into CCPNmr or Sparky software.
Adjust the counter level for an appropriate signal-to-noise ratio.
Perform automatic peak picking on the spectra.
Inspect all selected peaks and manually correct missed or incorrectly picked peaks.
Label the peaks with assigned residues based on previous assignments.
Copy assignments to the spectrum of apo-p62ZZ.
Adjust peak positions by tracing arginine-induced movement of crosspeaks.
Label the peaks with assigned residues on the spectrum of apo-formed p62ZZ.
Copy assignments to the spectrum of p62ZZ bound to dusquetide peptide or arginine amide at a molar ratio of 1:4.
Adjust peak positions based on titration experiments.
Output peak lists containing the 1H and 15N coordinates of individual peaks on the spectra.
Copy coordinates of the peaks in apo form and substrate-bound p62ZZ NMR spectra to a Microsoft Excel table.
Calculate observed CSPs in p62ZZ bound to substrates at a protein/ligand ratio of 1:4 relative to free state using the formula \( \frac{1}{2} (\delta_H^2 + \alpha \cdot \delta_N^2) \).
Determine δH and δN as differences in ppm between apo-formed and substrate-bound p62ZZ coordinates.
Set coefficient α to 0.2 for calculation.
Plot the histogram using residue numbers and CSPs in Excel.
Include p62ZZ domain amino acids 115–190 in plotting except for proline residues.
Indicate missing prolines with filled dots.
Treat unassigned residues as having a CSP value of zero and indicate them with filled squares.
Do not show CSPs for amino acids 174–190, which are less than 0.01 ppm.
Mark the threshold with a dash line to identify significantly perturbed residues.
Empirically determine the threshold based on each experiment.
Use one or two times the standard deviation as an initial threshold value.
Map the CSPs onto known p62ZZ protein structure in PyMol software.
Open the PDB file of p62ZZ in complex with dusquetide peptide.
Display the background in white color.
Present the p62ZZ protein as a surface in white.
Display the dusquetide peptide as sticks in pink.
Set the surface quality value to 2.
Select the most perturbed residues with CSPs above the threshold from the histogram.
Show these selected residues as a surface in pink.
Label the surface-exposed residues on the p62ZZ surface.
